2) Camila to share recommended embedding/reranker config and cost/latency tradeoffs (by Wed).
3) Marissa and Alex to align on procurement timeline and preferred support/SLA for Dedicated/Private options — Alex to loop procurement.

Thanks Marissa — this aligns with what we talked about. A couple quick clarifications from our engineering and security teams: 

- SDK & auth: we prefer examples for both server-side and client-side (browser) auth flows. We currently use AWS KMS and have a strict HSM-backed key policy for production.
- Routing: we want deterministic routing for critical paths (low latency) and fallback rules for cost savings. Can you show an example policy that falls back from a high-quality model to a quantized variant?
- Structured output / tool-calling: our support assistant needs JSON output for downstream ingestion; show best practices for tool-calling and validation against a schema.
- Embeddings/reranker: we'd like guidance on index size tradeoffs, approximate nearest neighbor configs, and examples of combining embeddings with an LLM reranker.
- Prompt governance: security asked for a high-level governance doc and examples of versioned system prompts + controls to prevent prompt injection. Also please include your red-team approach for prompt-level exploits.

I've added Priya (procurement) and security@acme.com to the thread. Priya — can you share target procurement timeline?

—Alex

From: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.com>
To: Alex Chen <alex.chen@acme.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Camila Reyes <camila@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 19 May 2026 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: Acme integration — SDK, auth, routing & prompt governance

Hi Alex — following up with the tech note and attachments. Long version in the attached 'redwood-sdk-quickstart.pdf' and 'prompt-governance-outline.docx', quick highlights below.

1) SDK setup & auth patterns\- Quickstart: server SDK (node/python) includes a single-line init using an API key or instance role for Dedicated/Private (see PDF).
- Server-side: recommended to keep private keys on the server; use short-lived tokens for client flows.
- KMS integration: Redwood supports AWS KMS and customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-key). For HSM-backed keys, we provide an HSM integration guide and audit hooks (see SOC2-evidence.zip).

2) Routing & model fallbacks\- Example routing policy: route by intent/latency bucket -> prefer high-quality model (redwood/gpt-qa-hero) for queries with safety or legal intents; fallback to quantized / distilled variant (gpt-qa-lite-q4) when latency > 200ms or throughput demands spike.
- Policy snippet (pseudo):
  - if intent in [legal, billing] => route to gpt-qa-hero (SLO 120ms)
  - else if token_cost_estimate > threshold => route to gpt-qa-lite-q4
  - fallback chain includes region-aware routing and capacity-tier fallback (dedicated -> hosted).

3) Structured output & tool-calling\- Use Redwood's structured output schema support: declare an output JSON schema and enable strict validation in the model call. When using tool-calling, wrap external tool responses with a verification step and reject responses that fail schema checks.
- Example: prompt instructs model to return {"action": "search", "query": "..."} and Redwood validates against the schema before downstream processing. We recommend a post-output validator and a short canonicalizer to enforce types.

4) Embeddings + reranker\- Recommended pattern: index with 1536-d embeddings, use HNSW with efConstruction tuned for index size, and run a light L2/INNER product approximate search to retrieve top-K candidates. Feed top 50 into a lightweight LLM reranker (2-4 shot prompts) for best precision.
- Cost/latency tradeoff: larger K raises recall but increases reranker cost; recommend storing document clustering metadata to pre-filter candidates. Camila will share concrete numbers.

5) Prompt templates & system prompt governance\- Versioning: store system prompts in a version-controlled repository (git) with semantic versions (v1.0.0). Each deployment binds to a specific prompt version hash. Include changelogs that list behavioral tests and eval prompts.
- Prompt injection mitigations: use input sanitization, strict output schemas, model-level token budgets for injected content, and prefix-only system prompts for sensitive instructions. Combine with runtime checks — e.g., compare output to baseline behavior for known injection patterns.
- Red teaming: run adversarial prompt suites (open- and closed-box) and include behavioral regression tests; log all failing cases and require a triage loop before a prompt version is promoted. We can provide an initial 500-sample adversarial prompt set for Acme.

Attachments (stubs): redwood-sdk-quickstart.pdf, prompt-governance-outline.docx, SOC2-evidence.zip

If you'd like, we can also share a short demo repo that shows embedding indexing -> ANN search -> reranking pipeline. Happy to schedule a 45-min deep-dive with your engineering team.

—Dylan
